EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) combined with an event-study (leads/lags) implemented with the Sun & Abraham (2020) estimator.  

Rationale  
• Manager moves are discrete, well-dated shocks that change only one explanatory factor—the identity (and traits) of the top executive—while keeping the firm, industry and macro environment constant.  
• Many firms switch managers at different calendar years → “staggered adoption.”  
• DiD lets us purge time-invariant firm heterogeneity (firm FE) and common shocks (year FE) while exploiting the before/after contrast within the same firm.  
• The event-study provides a visual/quantitative pre-trend test and dynamics of the effect.  
• Once we establish that “managers matter,” we interact treatment with observable traits (MBA, birth cohort dummies) to test whether those traits systematically shift policies.

Optional Extension  
Variance-decomposition AKM two-way FE (Abowd, Kramarz & Margolis 1999) to quantify the share of residual policy variation attributable to manager FE, but causal interpretation rests on the DiD above.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2. Treatment and Control  

2.1 Treatment variable  
Treated_it = 1 if firm i in year t employs a NEW incoming top manager j (CEO/CFO/other officer) whose first appearance at firm i is year t.  
For trait analyses we create:  
TreatedTrait_it = Treated_it × Trait_j (e.g., MBA_j =1, Cohort_1946-1955_j, etc.).

2.2 Control group / Counterfactual  
• “Not-yet-treated” or “never-treated” firms in the same calendar year with identical industry (2-digit SIC) and size tercile that have no top-executive change in a symmetric event window (−5, +5) supply contemporaneous trends.  
• Within-firm pre-period (−5 to −1) observations of the treated firms themselves supply an additional baseline.

2.3 Event date / timing  
Event year 0 = first fiscal year in which the incoming manager shows up on the firm’s top-officer list (for Execucomp a Named Executive; for Forbes file, any listed officer). Leads (k = −5,…,−1) and lags (k = 0,…,+5) are coded relative to that year.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: Absent the managerial move, the treated firm would have continued to follow the same trajectory as control firms.  
Plausibility: Same-industry, size-matched controls and firm FE absorb most structural differences; we will test for zero coefficients on leads k = −5,…,−2.

A2. No anticipation (or at least no behavioral change >1 year before appointment).  
Plausibility: Search processes are typically short and private; board deliberations are not public until close to appointment, making long-run anticipation unlikely.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): One firm’s hiring of a specific manager does not directly alter another control firm’s policies.  
Plausibility: Executive moves are idiosyncratic; only potential spillover is rival reaction in M&A markets, which we will address by dropping same-3-digit SIC rivals in robustness.

A4. Composition stability: Other top-management-team changes do not systematically coincide exactly with event timing in treated vs. control firms.  
Plausibility: We will verify and control for simultaneous CFO/COO turnover dummies.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  

T1. Endogenous matching / reverse causality  
   Threat: Boards may hire a “cost-cutter” exactly when they plan cost reductions.  
   Remedy:  
   • Include firm-specific linear (or flexible spline) time trends.  
   • Control for lagged outcome levels to soak up mean-reversion.  
   • Run an IV robustness: instrument the trait interaction with the leave-one-out average trait among managers that leave rival firms in the same year (“supply shock” of MBA managers).  

T2. Anticipatory adjustments in year −1  
   Remedy: drop t − 1 or collapse leads into (−2 to −5) and check robustness; main conclusions must hold when excluding t − 1.

T3. Simultaneous macro/industry shocks (e.g., defense spending booms that change both hiring and cap-ex)  
   Remedy: include industry×year FE and macro controls (GDP growth, Fed Funds, etc.); cluster SE at firm and 2-digit-SIC (two-way) to allow arbitrary serial and spatial correlation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# -------------------- 5.1 Load packages --------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # feols with Sun-Abraham
library(did)             # Callaway–Sant’Anna
library(sandwich)
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------- 5.2 Read and merge data --------------
firm <- fread("compustat_firmyear.csv")      # firm-level accounting
exec <- fread("exec_moves.csv")              # manager-firm-year panel
traits <- fread("manager_traits.csv")        # age, MBA, cohort etc.

# Merge manager traits onto exec, tag each first-year-at-firm
setkey(exec, manager_id, firm_id, fyear)
exec[, first_year := fyear == min(fyear), by = .(manager_id, firm_id)]
exec <- merge(exec, traits, by = "manager_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Keep only first-year rows for treatment definition
moves <- exec[first_year == TRUE, .(firm_id, fyear, manager_id, mba = MBA, cohort = birth_cohort)]
setnames(moves, "fyear", "event_year")

# -------------------- 5.3 Generate treatment dummies -------
# Expand moves back onto full firm-year panel
panel <- merge(firm, moves, by = c("firm_id"), all.x = TRUE, allow.cartesian = TRUE)

# Event time (k = year - event_year)
panel[, k := fyear - event_year]

# Treated indicator: treated from k>=0 onward
panel[, treated := as.integer(!is.na(event_year) & k >= 0)]

# Interaction with traits
panel[, treated_mba := treated * mba]
panel[, treated_cohort_46_55 := treated * as.integer(cohort == "1946-1955")]

# -------------------- 5.4 Keep clean window ---------------
panel <- panel[k >= -5 & k <= 5]  # 11-year window
panel[, post := (k >= 0)]

# -------------------- 5.5 Main DiD with SA estimator -------
feols(capex_assets ~ sunab(event_year, fyear) | firm_id + fyear, 
      cluster = ~firm_id + event_year,
      data = panel) -> est_event

# -------------------- 5.6 Trait interaction ---------------
feols(capex_assets ~ sunab(event_year, fyear, ref.p = -1) + treated_mba |
      firm_id + fyear, cluster = ~firm_id,
      data = panel) -> est_trait

# -------------------- 5.7 Robustness: firm-specific trends
panel[, fyear_rel := fyear - min(fyear), by = firm_id]
feols(capex_assets ~ sunab(event_year, fyear) + fyear_rel |
      firm_id + fyear, cluster = ~firm_id, data = panel) -> est_trend

# -------------------- 5.8 Plot event-study ---------------
iplot(est_event)

```

Key variable notes  
• capex_assets = capital expenditures / total assets (analogous specs for leverage, dividends, etc.).  
• All monetary variables winsorized at 1–99 %.  
• Standard errors two-way clustered by firm and manager (or firm and event year).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

6. Expected Results  

• We expect statistically significant manager fixed-effects, explaining ≈20 % of the residual variance in investment and financing ratios after removing firm, industry and year FE.  
• Average effect of a new manager arrival: |Δ| of 1–2 percentage-points of assets in cap-ex and 50–100 bp in leverage within two years.  
• MBAs: predicted to raise cash holdings and R&D (more “option value” mindset) and lower dividends (retain earnings).  
Magnitude: MBA arrival decreases payout ratio by ~5 ppt relative to non-MBA arrivals.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)  

C1: Parallel pre-trends supported by insignificant lead coefficients ….. 0.8  
C2: No anticipatory behavior ≥2 years before appointment ……………… 0.7  
C3: No time-varying confounders after controls + firm trends ………….. 0.6  
C4: No spillovers across control units (SUTVA) ………………………………. 0.8  
C5: Correct inference (two-way clustering, SA estimator) ………………. 1.0  

Average score ≈ 0.78 – credible but not bullet-proof; most residual concern is endogenous matching (C3).
